reverse_outline.summary: Three-point preview: one owner per promise, same stories on two architectures, events for operations and batches for finance with keys and reconciliation
Systems can each be right yet disagree; this part follows orders across handoffs at a fictional brand
Thesis: journeys break at handoffs, and hold with one writer per fact plus keys and reconciliation
Roadmap of the four stories: consumer order, exchange, wholesale reorder, Black Friday
Method: fixed order data run on the improved Waypoint systems, then compared with the January 2027 landscape
The comparison shows stock and orders need events while invoices and payouts can be batched
Preview of the consumer order journey from search to accounting
Preview of the return-and-exchange journey and its refund branch
Preview of the wholesale EDI reorder and why shipment notices must match packing
Preview of the Black Friday 2026 failure and the 2027 peak plan
Callback to the opening question and pointer to start with the consumer order chapter

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
Every unit's outline summary matches the controlling idea of its aligned spec paragraph (p01-p10); the KEY POINTS callout matches no spec paragraph and is declared in the spec as evidence of p02.

Only Introduction ¶4 was marked two_ideas (the Waypoint setting and the chapter shape); the spec's p04 controlling idea declares exactly that pairing as one idea (the setting and layout the comparison is told in), and the paragraph holds to it. All other units have one idea.
Each unit traces to the thesis: p01 hook, p02 claim (P9-5), p03/p04 roadmap and setting, p05 event-versus-batch part of the claim, p06-p09 to P9-1..P9-4 with P9-5, p10 synthesis.
The KEY POINTS callout, Figures 1-3 (each with an explanatory caption; Figure 3 referenced in the text) and the scenario figures in the chapter paragraphs each state what they show.
cause_effect: 'Run on the systems ... each of these journeys broke at a handoff' states what following the walkthroughs of ¶1 shows.
example: 'Four stories show it.' carries the claim and introduces the stories.
elaboration: 'The first three journeys keep the dates and amounts of April 2027 orders' carries the first three stories into their setting.
elaboration: 'The comparison shows which handoffs must be fast.' carries the January 2027 comparison of ¶4.
elaboration (phrase): the heading and the chapter-by-chapter paragraphs elaborate the four stories in the announced order.
sequence: 'follows the jacket's M-to-L exchange' carries Eva's order into its return.
contrast: 'changes the buyer' marks the business buyer against the consumer order.
sequence: 'puts the consumer path under peak load' carries the first chapter's path.
conclusion_summary: 'Each journey turns the opening's parcel ... into a question' sums the chapters and returns to the opening.

results.quote: each of these journeys broke at a handoff, not inside a system
results.finding: Both flow readers lost the antecedent of 'these journeys': ¶1 speaks of 'these four walkthroughs' and the journeys are named only in ¶3, so the claim seems to refer to journeys not yet met. Naming them as the walkthroughs of ¶1 (or the four journeys of this part) at the boundary would fix it without reordering.
results.corroborated_by: flowB, item 3 bullet 1 ('"these journeys" points back to walkthroughs I have not met yet'); first reader flowA, item 3 bullet 1

results.quote: Run on the systems Kestrel & Pine had in January 2027, and on Black Friday 2026
results.finding: Both flow readers met 'the systems Kestrel & Pine had in January 2027' before learning there is a second, late-2027 architecture (¶4), and read the claim as saying the book's own journeys break. Both propose moving the two-landscape setup (the first sentence of ¶4) before or into the claim. The difficulty comes from the declared order (claim before setting), which the spec chose deliberately from round-1 readers; a phrase in ¶2 marking January 2027 as the earlier landscape might suffice, so the fault is unclear.
results.corroborated_by: flowB, item 3 bullet 1 ('I also read it as saying the book's journeys break, until P4') and item 4; first reader flowA, item 3 bullet 1 and item 4

results.quote: keep the dates and amounts of April 2027 orders but run them on the systems Kestrel & Pine has from late 2027
results.finding: Both flow readers had to re-read to separate the time points (January 2027, April 2027, late 2027, Black Friday 2026) and see that the April orders are replayed on later systems; the sentence does not say it is a replay.
results.corroborated_by: flowB, item 3 bullet 3; first reader flowA, item 3 bullet 2

results.quote: The comparison shows which handoffs must be fast.
results.finding: Both flow readers found the event-versus-batch rule a new topic rather than a consequence of the claim: the claim paragraph (¶2) speaks only of writers, keys and reconciliation, and speed appears before ¶5 only in the KEY POINTS. Both suggest setting it up in the claim paragraph, which the spec's p02 controlling idea does not include (the thesis_statement places event versus batch in p05 only), so the remedy is a spec change.
results.corroborated_by: flowB, item 2 P5 ('it adds a new idea (event vs batch) rather than following up on P2'); first reader flowA, item 3 bullet 3 and item 4

results.finding: Both flow readers stumbled on the capitalised incident names (Double Refund, ASN Chargeback) given with no plain description. The audience is declared to know these incidents, but the spec's AC-1 expected answer uses plain descriptions ('January's duplicate-payment failure', 'an earlier €14,200 deduction'); a few plain words beside each name would remove the stumble.
results.corroborated_by: flowB, item 3 bullet 4; first reader flowA, item 3 bullet 4

results.quote: Three pallets arrive on 9 April; payment is due 9 May.
results.finding: Both flow readers noted the missing year; the second read 9 April as out of sequence with Eva's 13 April order. Stating the year (and that it precedes Eva's order) would fix it.
results.corroborated_by: flowB, item 3 bullet 5; first reader flowA, item 3 bullet 5

results.quote: what changes between the January 2027 landscape and Waypoint is whether the promises hold
results.finding: One flow reader (flowB, item 3 bullet 2) found Waypoint and 'the January 2027 landscape' unexplained in the KEY POINTS; Waypoint is defined only in ¶4. Not reported by flowA.

results.quote: The ASN Chargeback's €14,200 deduction explains why the notice must describe actual packing.
results.finding: The terms reader could not connect 'pallet notice' / 'wholesale shipment notices' to the ASN in 'ASN Chargeback'; the incident is on already_knows, but the draft never says the pallet notice is the ASN, so the incident's relevance is lost.
results.corroborated_by: flowA, item 3 bullet 4 and flowB, item 3 bullet 4 (both report 'ASN' unexpanded and guessed it is the pallet notice)

results.quote: what changes between the January 2027 landscape and Waypoint
results.finding: 'Landscape' (the systems in place at a date) is used in the KEY POINTS before the body explains it in ¶2 and ¶4.
results.corroborated_by: flowB, item 3 bullet 2 ('KEY POINTS bullet 2 uses "Waypoint" and "the January 2027 landscape" with no explanation')

results.quote: an **order management system** for shared orders
results.finding: 'Shared orders' does not say what the orders are shared between (channels, D2C and B2B).

results.quote: gives each protective action and recovery check an owner
results.finding: 'Protective action and recovery check' is too vague for the terms reader to work out: protective against what, checking which recovery.

results.quote: The same four stories run on two architectures.
results.finding: 'The same four stories' and 'operations by event, finance by batch' in the KEY POINTS precede the paragraphs that name the stories (¶3) and explain event versus batch (¶5).
Opens on a puzzling scenario (parcel shipped versus being prepared), not a dictionary definition, sweeping generalisation or announcement.
The conclusion does not restate the chapters; it turns the opening's parcel into a question and gives a starting point.
Synthesis: each journey asks which system owns the fact and how the other learns it; so-what: the question can be checked in any landscape.
'the opening's parcel, shipped yet being prepared' names the hook of ¶1 again.

The intro-only reader named the four chapters in the roadmap's order with the January 2027 comparison and the peak's two settings; the AC-1 reader's answer matches the expected answer on every chapter (order #1072455 details, M-to-L exchange 19/22 April and the refund branch, Bergzicht's 240 units, €19,860, 9 April/9 May, €14,200, Black Friday's backlog, 1,340 units, €96,000 and the 2027 plan).

The AC-2 reader says the dates and amounts stay fixed so only whether the promises hold changes, names scheduled stock copies as the earlier failure, and lists what to look at: the owner of each fact, one writer, idempotency keys and daily reconciliation. Matches expected.
